prompt: Which part of a commit is the only one that can say why a change was made?
hint: The diff shows what; the date shows when.

choices.why: It shows what changed, not the problem it solved.
Who, not why.
It identifies the commit and explains nothing.
Right. Nothing else in a commit can hold a reason.

prompt: Which is the best first line for a commit that changes the opening time for the winter?
hint: It should complete: If applied, this commit will…

choices.why: It does not say what was fixed; the reader has to open the commit.
It says where, which the diff already shows, and not what or why.

choices.text: Open at half past six from October to March
choices.why: Right. Imperative, short, and it says the one thing.
Not the imperative, and a full stop on a title.

prompt: What belongs in the body of a commit message?
hint: The diff already shows the lines.

choices.text: A list of the lines that changed
choices.why: The diff shows that exactly; repeating it adds nothing.
Right. The problem it solved, and what it deliberately left alone.

choices.text: The author's name and the date
choices.why: Git records both already.
The id is computed from the message, so it cannot be in it.

prompt: A message's first line is kept to around ___ characters, because lists of commits cut it off.
Match each part of feat(order)!: require a pickup time to what it says.
hint: One description is not part of the first line.

pairs.right: It breaks something that used to work

prompt: Since v1.4.2 there have been two fix commits and one feat commit, none with ! or BREAKING CHANGE. What is the next version?
hint: The biggest kind of change decides.

choices.why: That would be fixes only; a feat moves the middle number.
Only a breaking change moves the first number.
Right. Something new, nothing broken.
Versions count releases, not commits.

prompt: What does git log --oneline --grep="^feat" v1.0..HEAD list?
hint: ^ means the start of the message.

choices.text: Every commit whose message mentions feat anywhere
choices.why: ^ anchors it to the start.
Right. Half of the release notes, from the history.
v1.0..HEAD is what came after it.
Those are marked by ! or BREAKING CHANGE, not by feat alone.

prompt: fix: fix bug follows Conventional Commits exactly. What is wrong with it?
hint: A type is not a reason.

choices.text: Nothing; it is in the format
choices.why: The format is satisfied and the reader learns nothing.

choices.text: fix is not a type the specification allows
choices.why: fix is one of the two the specification defines.
The scope is optional.

choices.text: It says nothing about what was fixed
choices.why: Right. The convention structures a message; it does not write one.

prompt: Besides the !, a footer states what breaks. It begins BREAKING ___:

choices.why: That is git add .; -p asks about each hunk.
Nothing leaves the machine; it only stages.
Right. It stages the ones you accept. y stages it, n leaves it.

choices.text: Creates a patch file for email
choices.why: Patch here means a piece of a change, and nothing is written to a file.

prompt: A single commit raised the price of bread and changed the opening days. A week later the price rise must be undone. What goes wrong with git revert?

choices.text: It also undoes the opening days
choices.why: Right. Two changes in one commit can only be reverted together.
It reverts any commit.

choices.text: It deletes the commit from the history
choices.why: revert adds a commit; lesson 4.

choices.text: Nothing; revert picks the lines about prices
choices.why: It cannot tell which lines were about what.

prompt: Match each answer to git add -p's question to what it does.
hint: One description is something add -p never does.

prompt: git commit --fixup HEAD~1 made a commit. What does its message say?
hint: It names the commit it belongs with.

choices.text: fixup!, then the first line of the other commit
choices.why: Right. --autosquash later reads it to know where it belongs.

choices.text: Nothing; fixup commits have empty messages
choices.why: It has a message, and the message is the point.
Git writes it; no editor opens.
It names the commit by message, not by id.

prompt: Ana's branch has a fixup! commit, and Bruno has already reviewed the branch's commits on the pull request. Should she run git rebase -i --autosquash now?

choices.text: Yes, since the result is tidier
choices.why: Tidier, and rewritten under a reviewer who has already read the old ones.

choices.text: Yes, autosquash does not change ids
choices.why: It rewrites commits, and they get new ids.

choices.text: No; add new commits and let the merge button decide
choices.why: Right. Once shared, rewriting follows lesson 6's rule.

choices.text: No, fixup commits can only be squashed by the reviewer
choices.why: Anybody can squash; the question is when.

prompt: To fold every fixup! commit into the commit it names: git rebase -i ___ HEAD~3
hint: auto, then the word for combining.

prompt: Put the parts of a Conventional Commits message in order, top to bottom.
hint: The first line has the type.
trap: The footer comes last; putting it first hides the description.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about the format, not the content.

choices.text: A first line should complete: If applied, this commit will…
choices.why: Yes. That is the imperative.

choices.text: Following Conventional Commits guarantees a good message
choices.why: fix: fix bug is in the format.

choices.text: One change per commit makes revert precise
choices.why: Yes. It undoes that change and no other.

choices.text: Most commits need a long body
choices.why: Most need none; the ones whose reason is not obvious do.

choices.text: Tidying commits before sharing is safe
choices.why: Yes. Nobody else has them yet.
